# Status report: jf2 allocator test in kestrel, 2026-11-20

## Short version

- jf2 (our fork of the jemalloc memory allocator) reduced the latency spikes in kestrel (our key-value store).
- On a read-heavy workload, p99 latency (the level 99% of requests stay under) fell from 2140 to 870 microseconds.
- Memory use rose by 5.7 GB (9.3%), and the capacity team has not yet approved that increase.

## Words used here

- **kestrel**: our key-value store. It is the program under test.
- **jemalloc**: an open-source memory allocator library.
- **jf2**: our fork of jemalloc 5.3.
- **bench-07**: the test host.
- **Latency spike**: a short period when requests take much longer than usual.
- **p50, p99, p99.9**: latency percentiles. For example, 99% of requests finish within the p99 latency.
- **us**: microseconds. **kops/s**: thousand operations per second.
- **YCSB**: Yahoo! Cloud Serving Benchmark, a standard benchmark for key-value stores. YCSB-B is its read-heavy workload (standard mix: 95% reads, 5% updates). YCSB-A is its write-heavy workload (standard mix: 50% reads, 50% updates).
- **RSS**: resident set size. It is the physical memory that the process holds.
- **Decay purge**: jemalloc returns unused memory to the operating system after a delay.
- **perf**: the Linux profiler. **je_arena_decay** is the jemalloc function that runs the decay purge.
- **Load average**: the average number of tasks running or waiting for a CPU.
- **NUMA pinning**: binding threads to the CPUs and memory of one socket.
- **logrotate**: a system tool that archives log files. **cron** is the system job scheduler that starts it.
- **Staging**: the pre-production environment.

## Test setup

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Host | bench-07: 2 x 32-core Xeon, 512 GB memory, kernel 6.8 |
| Load before the runs | load average 0.4 (under 1% of 64 cores busy) |
| Build A | commit 4f1c2aa of main, with jemalloc 5.3 |
| Build B | commit 4f1c2aa of main, with jf2 |
| Workload | YCSB-B, 64 client threads |
| Run length | 10 minutes per run |
| Run count | 5 runs per build, alternating A, B, A, B, ... |

## Results

```
Median of 5 runs. One block = 200 us. Lower is better.

p99    A  ███████████ 2140 us
       B  ████ 870 us                    59% lower
p99.9  A  █████████████████████████████████████████████████ 9800 us
       B  ████████████████ 3100 us       68% lower
```

Only p99 and p99.9 changed. Throughput and p50 stayed within the run-to-run range.

| Metric | Build A (jemalloc 5.3) | Build B (jf2) | Change in median |
|---|---|---|---|
| Throughput, kops/s | 412 (405 to 418) | 409 (401 to 415) | -3 kops/s (-0.7%) |
| p50 latency, us | 118 (116 to 121) | 119 (117 to 121) | +1 us (+0.8%) |
| p99 latency, us | 2140 (1890 to 2610) | 870 (820 to 940) | -1270 us (-59%) |
| p99.9 latency, us | 9800 (7200 to 14100) | 3100 (2700 to 3900) | -6700 us (-68%) |
| RSS at end, GB | 61.2 | 66.9 | +5.7 GB (+9.3%) |

Each cell shows the median of 5 runs, then the lowest and highest run. RSS has one value per build and no range.

## What the data shows

- p99 latency is 59% lower with jf2. The two ranges do not overlap. The lowest A value is 1890 us, and the highest B value is 940 us [Ref1].
- p99.9 latency is 68% lower with jf2. These ranges do not overlap either. The lowest A value is 7200 us, and the highest B value is 3900 us [Ref1].
- B varies less between runs. The p99 range is 120 us wide for B and 720 us wide for A [Ref1].
- Throughput and p50 show no measurable change. The medians differ by less than 1%, and the A and B ranges overlap [Ref1].
- RSS at the end of the run is 5.7 GB (9.3%) higher with jf2 [Ref1].

## Likely cause of the spikes

- The spikes in build A occur at the same times as the decay purge. In the spike windows, 31% of the perf samples are in je_arena_decay [Ref2].
- jf2 runs the purge in a background thread.
- Hypothesis: the purge on the request threads causes the spikes in A. The lower p99 in B is consistent with this. A perf profile of B during its slowest windows would confirm or reject it.

## One B run was replaced

- Run 3 of build B stalled for 40 s at minute 7.
- The cause was the nightly logrotate cron job, not the allocator [Ref3].
- The run was repeated. The B results above use the repeat and exclude the stalled run.

## Not tested

- YCSB-A, the write-heavy workload
- more than 64 client threads
- NUMA pinning

The results apply only to YCSB-B at 64 client threads without NUMA pinning.

## Open question

Is the RSS increase of 5.7 GB (9.3%) acceptable? The capacity team must approve it.

## Next steps

1. Run YCSB-A tomorrow (2026-11-21).
2. Ask the capacity team to approve the RSS increase.
3. If they approve, enable jf2 in staging with a feature flag (a switch to turn it off).

## References

- [Ref1] Results table in this report. It covers 5 runs per build on bench-07, 2026-11-20, with one B run repeated.
- [Ref2] perf profile of build A during the spike windows, same test.
- [Ref3] Investigation of the 40 s stall in run 3 of build B, same test.

---

Items I added that are not in your notes. Check them before you send the report:

- The YCSB mixes (95% reads and 5% updates for B, 50% and 50% for A) are the standard definitions. Confirm that your configuration matches.
- I labeled the purge explanation a hypothesis and proposed the perf profile of B as the confirming measurement. Your notes do not say whether B was profiled.
- The statement that RSS has no range reflects only what the notes contain.
